one_liner: Portable C hash family (t1ha0/1/2) beating xxHash/Murmur on bulk throughput; modest edge on tiny keys.
what_it_does: t1ha ('Fast Positive Hash') is a family of non-cryptographic hash functions for hash tables, checksums, and fingerprinting: t1ha1 (64-bit, stable across platforms), t1ha2 (64- or 128-bit, streaming-capable, the recommended variant), and t1ha0 (64-bit, dispatches at runtime to the fastest implementation for the current CPU, including AES-NI/AVX paths on x86 and dedicated 32-bit/big-endian variants). It is a plain C API, not a std::hash drop-in: you call e.g. t1ha2_atonce(data, length, seed) directly and get a uint64_t back, or use the t1ha2_init/update/final trio for streaming; wiring it into std::unordered_map means writing your own hash functor.
how_it_is_fast: The t1ha0_ia32aes_* variants use AES-NI instructions for hardware-accelerated mixing (this is the 't1ha_aes' benchmark line); each AES-NI variant is compiled with its own flags (-maes plus -mavx/-mavx2 per meson.build) and t1ha0 picks among them, plus 32-bit and big-endian fallbacks, at runtime via T1HA0_RUNTIME_SELECT (optionally using GNU ELF indirect functions to cut call overhead). The core mixing uses a NH/UMAC-style multiply-add construction that the README's FAQ says was deliberately fixed to avoid the 'blinding multiplication' entropy-loss flaw it attributes to plain NH-family designs (and, per the README, to wyhash).
when_to_use: Bulk hashing of large buffers (KB+: checksums, content fingerprinting, dedup) on x86_64 with AES-NI, where the 2016 SMHasher bulk numbers show t1ha_aes far ahead of xxHash32/64
Need a single API that gives both a 64-bit and a 128-bit digest via the same streaming context (t1ha2_init/update/final)
Already a portable C (not C++) codebase, or need a C-callable hash with existing Rust/Erlang/Go/Kotlin bindings (linked from the README)
Willing to vendor a small, frozen, Zlib-licensed source drop (3 .c files) since no upstream fixes are coming
Mixed/heterogeneous CPU fleet where t1ha0's automatic best-available-implementation dispatch is worth its small indirection cost
when_not_to_use: Tiny keys (a few bytes to ~31 bytes) on a modern CPU: the maintainer's own later self-check (i7-4600U, GCC 9.3, in the README) shows t1ha2_atonce at 17.25 cycles/hash already behind xxhash32 (16.55), xxh3_64 (15.1) and wyhash_v7 (14.1) -- the 2016 small-key win over xxHash32 was only ~1.2-1.3x and has since been erased by newer hashes
Cryptographic or adversarial-input use: the header explicitly states 't1ha' is 'Not suitable for cryptography'; no hash-flood resistance is claimed

Need active upstream maintenance: GitHub deleted the author's account in 2022 and this repo is a restored read-only mirror; the true origin moved to GitFlic, whose current activity is unverified (a GitFlic fetch timed out during verification)
Need std::hash-style implicit drop-in: t1ha is an explicit C function call with a seed argument, not something ADL or template specialization picks up automatically

About to reach for t1ha0_32le/32be or t1ha0_ia32aes without checking the table: the author flags several dispatch targets ('alien' 32-bit/big-endian variants) as niche, and picking the wrong one can be slower than a portable hash

integration.form: source-drop (3 .c files from /src, or link as a static/shared lib via the provided Makefile/meson.build/vcxproj)
integration.dependencies: none (pure C, standard headers only: stdint.h, stddef.h, limits.h)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (meson.build passes -std=c99); README recommends GNU C 5.5+, Clang 5.0+, or MSVC 2017 15.6+ for proper performance, older GNU C / VS2013+ also supported
integration.platforms: any CPU with native 64-bit arithmetic (portable fallback); accelerated paths for x86/x86_64 (AES-NI, AVX/AVX2) and Elbrus/e2k; separate 32-bit little/big-endian and 64-bit big-endian variants exist but are marked non-primary
integration.thread_safety: not documented explicitly; the hash functions are pure with no shared mutable state, and the streaming API uses a caller-allocated t1ha_context_t, so independent contexts are safe to use from different threads concurrently
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false -- explain: you call t1ha2_atonce(data, length, seed) (or t1ha1/t1ha0 equivalents) directly with an explicit seed, and must wrap it yourself to plug into std::hash-based containers

gotchas: t1ha0's chosen implementation depends on the host CPU's detected features, so its output is not guaranteed reproducible across machines; the README says t1ha0 results should only be used at runtime, never persisted or sent over a network -- use t1ha1/t1ha2 for stable, portable results
t1ha2_atonce's 64-bit result and t1ha2_atonce128's 128-bit result are unrelated values (the 64-bit hash is not a truncation of the 128-bit one), per the header comment

t1ha1 is documented to fail the strict avalanche criterion in some cases (per the README, discovered via Reini Urban's SMHasher fork); it is kept for compatibility but t1ha2 is the recommended, higher-quality successor

The AES-NI variants need per-file compiler flags (-maes plus -mavx/-mavx2), not just runtime CPU detection -- building them without the matching flags for your toolchain silently loses the AES-NI path
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick t1ha over MUM/VMUM, rapidhash, komihash, or CityHash when you specifically want the AES-NI bulk-throughput path on x86, a plain-C (not C++) implementation with existing Rust/Go/Erlang/Kotlin ports, or a Zlib license; the MUM/VMUM sibling entry directly reports beating t1ha2, and rapidhash/komihash report better small-key numbers than xxHash on modern CPUs, so for tiny-key or newest-hardware workloads check those siblings first.
verified_claims_summary: On SMHasher speed tests run in 2016 (GCC 5.4.0, -march=native -O3 -fPIC, Intel Core i7-6700K), t1ha_aes averaged 33.03 cycles/hash and t1ha 35.55 vs xxHash32's 43.72 over 1-31 byte keys (~1.2-1.3x fewer cycles), while on a 262144-byte bulk block t1ha_aes reached 34,636 MiB/s and t1ha 12,229 MiB/s vs xxHash32's 5,514 MiB/s (~6.3x/~2.2x) and xxHash64's 11,123 MiB/s (~3.1x/~1.1x). The verification pass found the source record had mislabeled those bulk MiB/s figures as the 'small keys' result; the real small-key edge over xxHash32 is only ~1.2-1.3x.
status_note: GitHub lists this repo as abandoned/archived, but per its own README that's because GitHub deleted the author's account in 2022 and this is a restored read-only mirror -- the stated true origin moved to GitFlic, whose activity level is unverified. Zlib-licensed and small (3 .c files), so it is cheap to vendor and self-maintain regardless.
